title: AQA GCSE Chemistry · The Periodic Table

items.stem: In the modern periodic table the elements are set out one after another in order of which quantity?

options.text: Atomic (proton) number, going up by one at each step
Relative atomic mass, the larger number in each box
The number of occupied electron shells it has
Number of neutrons in the nucleus of an atom

items.why: The specification states that the elements are arranged in order of atomic (proton) number, and that number climbs by one at every step.

items.stem: Before protons, neutrons and electrons were discovered, how did scientists attempt to classify the elements?

options.text: By arranging them in order of the atomic number
By arranging them in order of their outer electron counts
By arranging them in order of their atomic weights
By arranging them in order of their neutron count

items.why: The specification states that before those particles were known, scientists classified elements by ordering them by atomic weight.

items.stem: Which statement correctly describes where metals and non-metals sit in the periodic table?

options.text: Most elements are metals, on the left and lower down
Most elements are metals, on the right near the top
Most elements are non-metals, on the left and lower down
Most elements are non-metals, over on the right

items.why: The majority of elements are metals, found to the left and towards the bottom, with non-metals towards the right and top.

items.stem: What happens to the boiling points of the noble gases as relative atomic mass increases down Group 0?

options.text: They increase steadily going further down the group
They decrease as the gases become lighter down it
They stay the same, as these gases are stable
They fall sharply, halving with each step down

items.why: The specification states that the boiling points of the noble gases increase with increasing relative atomic mass.

items.stem: The Group 1 elements are known as the alkali metals. Which feature of their atoms gives them their characteristic properties?

options.text: Their atoms each hold just a single occupied electron shell
Their atoms each need a single electron more to fill a shell
Their atoms each have a single electron in the outer shell
Their atoms each have a single proton in the nucleus

items.why: Group 1 elements have characteristic properties because of the single electron in their outer shell.

items.stem: A small piece of potassium is dropped onto water. What are the products of the reaction?

options.text: Potassium oxide and hydrogen gas are both formed
Potassium chloride and hydrogen gas are given off
Potassium oxide and oxygen gas are given off
Potassium hydroxide and hydrogen gas form

items.why: A Group 1 metal reacts with water to give a metal hydroxide and hydrogen: 2K + 2H2O gives 2KOH + H2.

items.stem: Lithium is burned in oxygen, and separately sodium is burned in chlorine. What are the two products?

options.text: Lithium oxide and covalent sodium chloride molecules
Lithium oxide, Li2O, and sodium chloride, NaCl, are made
Lithium hydroxide and sodium chloride solution
Lithium oxide, LiO, plus sodium chloride, NaCl2

items.why: Group 1 metals burn in oxygen to give the metal oxide and in chlorine to give the metal chloride: 4Li + O2 gives 2Li2O.

items.stem: Which statement correctly describes the elements of Group 7, the halogens?

options.text: Non-metals with seven outer electrons, found as pairs
Non-metals with seven outer electrons, existing as atoms
Metals with seven outer electrons, going about in pairs
Non-metals with seven electron shells, joined in pairs

items.why: The halogens are non-metals with seven electrons in the outer shell, and they consist of molecules made of pairs of atoms.

items.stem: Why is the table of the elements described as periodic?

options.text: Because the table is revised at regular periods as new elements appear
Because elements with similar properties recur at regular intervals
Because every row repeats the properties of the row above it
Because each element repeats the electron count before it

items.why: The specification says the table is called periodic because similar properties occur at regular intervals along it.

items.stem: Chlorine and bromine are both in Group 7 and react in similar ways. What do atoms of these two elements share?

options.text: The same total number of electrons in the whole atom
The same number of occupied shells in the atom
The same number of outer electrons in an atom
The same number of neutrons in the nucleus

items.why: Elements in one group have the same number of outer electrons, and that is what gives them similar chemical properties.

items.stem: What problem arose in the early periodic tables when the strict order of atomic weights was followed?

options.text: Faulty weight values scattered elements far from their true partners
The atomic weights themselves had all been measured wrongly
Permanent gaps appeared that no element could ever fill
Some elements were placed in groups they did not belong in

items.why: The specification states that early tables were incomplete and that strict weight order put some elements in inappropriate groups.

items.stem: Mendeleev left gaps in his periodic table. Why did he do this?

options.text: He expected undiscovered elements to fill them
He believed that no element could ever exist there
He thought those places in nature were forever empty
He was unsure of several measured atomic weights

items.why: Mendeleev overcame some of the problems by leaving gaps for elements he thought had not yet been discovered.

items.stem: Knowledge of isotopes helped chemists understand the periodic table. What exactly did it explain?

options.text: Why atomic weights could be measured far more precisely
Why two atoms of one element hold different protons
Why an order based on atomic weights is not always correct
Why Mendeleev's swapped pairs were mistakes after all

items.why: Isotope mixtures mean atomic weight does not always rise with proton number, which explains the pairs Mendeleev had to swap.

items.stem: Sodium reacts to form Na+ ions and sulfur does not form positive ions. What does this tell you about them?

options.text: Sodium is a non-metal and sulfur is a metal
Sodium must be a non-metal, because it forms a positive ion
Both are non-metals, since neither formed a negative ion
Sodium is a metal and sulfur is a non-metal element

items.why: Elements that react to form positive ions are metals; elements that do not form positive ions are non-metals.

items.stem: Which pair of properties would you expect a typical metal to show, in contrast to a typical non-metal?

options.text: A poor conductor of heat that forms negative ions
A good heat conductor that forms positive ions
A good conductor of heat, yet it forms negative ions
A poor conductor of heat which forms positive ions

items.why: Metals conduct heat and electricity well and react to form positive ions; typical non-metals do neither.

items.stem: Why does magnesium react to form Mg2+ ions while chlorine reacts to form Cl- ions?

options.text: Magnesium loses its two outer electrons; chlorine gains one
Magnesium gains six electrons and chlorine loses seven
Magnesium has more protons than chlorine has in total
Magnesium has outer electrons it readily gives away

items.why: Reactions follow the arrangement of electrons: an atom with few outer electrons loses them, one with a nearly full shell gains.

items.stem: The noble gases in Group 0 are unreactive. Which statement explains this and describes their outer shells?

options.text: Their outer shells are empty, so there is nothing left to react
Their arrangements are stable, eight outer but two in helium
Every one of them holds exactly eight electrons in the outer shell
They travel as pairs, so their bonds are already used

items.why: Noble gases are unreactive because their atoms have stable electron arrangements: eight outer electrons, or two in helium.

items.stem: Argon has the electronic structure 2,8,8. Why does argon not easily form molecules?

options.text: It has already shared its electrons within a pair
Its atoms already exist joined together in pairs
Its outer shell is stable, so it need not share
Its outer shell has no electrons available to share

items.why: With a stable outer arrangement, argon has no tendency to gain, lose or share electrons, so it does not easily form molecules.

items.stem: Why does the reactivity of the Group 1 metals increase going down the group?

options.text: Atoms lower down have many more electrons to give away
Atoms lower down have more protons pulling on the shell
Atoms lower down need to gain fewer electrons
The outer electron is further out, so easily lost

items.why: Going down the group the outer electron is further from the nucleus and more shielded, so the attraction is weaker and it is lost more easily.

items.stem: Chlorine reacts with sodium, and separately with hydrogen. What kinds of compound are formed?

options.text: An ionic compound with sodium, and ions with hydrogen too
A covalent compound with sodium, and ions with hydrogen
An ionic compound with sodium, and a molecule with hydrogen
A covalent compound in both, since chlorine is a non-metal

items.why: A halogen with a metal gives an ionic metal halide, NaCl; with a non-metal it gives a covalent molecule, HCl.

items.stem: Why does the reactivity of the halogens decrease going down Group 7?

options.text: The outer shell is further out, so gaining one is harder
Larger atoms are heavier, so they must react more sluggishly
Extra shells lower down leave fewer outer electrons exposed
Atoms lower down lose their outer electrons more easily

items.why: Going down the group the outer shell is further from the nucleus and more shielded, so an electron is attracted and gained less easily.

items.stem: An atom of element X has the electronic structure 2,8,7. Where in the periodic table is X found?

options.text: Group 3 and Period 7, reading its three occupied shells
Group 17 and Period 3, counting all the electrons
Group 3 and Period 3, since the shell count gives both
Group 7 and Period 3, from seven outer electrons

items.why: Seven electrons in the outer shell places X in Group 7, and three occupied shells places it in Period 3.

items.stem: Rubidium lies below potassium in Group 1. From its position, what can be predicted about its reaction with water?

options.text: It reacts less vigorously than potassium, being a heavier metal
It reacts more vigorously than potassium, giving off hydrogen gas
It reacts to give rubidium oxide along with hydrogen gas
It reacts much like strontium, its neighbour in that period

items.why: Reactivity increases down Group 1, so rubidium reacts more vigorously than potassium and gives rubidium hydroxide and hydrogen.

items.stem: Magnesium has the electronic structure 2,8,2. How does this relate to its position in the periodic table?

options.text: Two outer electrons put it in Group 2, on the right
Two outer electrons put it in Group 2, identical to calcium
Two outer electrons make it a non-metal in Group 2
Two outer electrons put it in Group 2, among the metals

items.why: Two outer electrons place magnesium in Group 2, on the left of the table, where elements lose electrons to form positive ions.

items.stem: Boiling points in Group 0 are helium -269 C, neon -246 C, argon -186 C. Predict the boiling point of krypton.

options.text: Below -269 C, continuing past helium at the top
About -153 C, carrying the rise further down
About -230 C, falling below argon down the group
About -246 C, the same value as neon shows

items.why: Boiling points increase down Group 0, so krypton, below argon, must boil at a higher temperature than -186 C.

items.stem: Lithium reacts steadily with water, sodium melts into a ball and potassium bursts into flame. Predict how caesium behaves.

options.text: Less vigorously than lithium, being the heaviest metal here
About the same as potassium, as both are in Group 1
Even more vigorously than potassium, reacting explosively
Steadily, because its outer electron is held tightly

items.why: Reactivity increases down Group 1, so caesium, well below potassium, reacts more violently still.

items.stem: Melting points in Group 7 are chlorine -101 C, bromine -7 C, iodine 114 C. Predict the melting point of astatine.

options.text: About -150 C, since reactivity falls down the group
About -90 C, dropping since reactivity falls
About 114 C, matching iodine in the group
About 300 C, continuing the rise on below iodine

items.why: Melting and boiling points increase down Group 7 as relative molecular mass increases, so astatine melts above iodine.

items.stem: Chlorine solution is added to colourless potassium bromide solution. What is observed, and why?

options.text: No change, as bromine is the more reactive halogen
It turns orange, as bromine has been displaced
It turns orange as bromine displaces the chlorine
No change, since both elements sit in the same group

items.why: Chlorine is more reactive than bromine, so it displaces bromine from the solution of its salt: Cl2 + 2KBr gives 2KCl + Br2.

items.stem: An atom of element Z has 15 protons. Where in the periodic table is Z found?

options.text: Group 5 and Period 3, from five outer electrons
Group 3 and Period 5, counting its three shells
Group 15 and Period 3, adding all its electrons
Group 5 and Period 5, both from the outer shell

items.why: 15 protons means 15 electrons, arranged 2,8,5. Five outer electrons give Group 5 and three occupied shells give Period 3.

items.stem: An atom of element Q has 19 protons. What does an atom of Q do when it reacts?

options.text: Loses one electron to form a 1+ ion
Loses its outer electron, giving a 1- ion
Gains seven electrons to form a 7- ion
Loses four electrons to make a 4+ ion

items.why: 19 protons means 19 electrons, arranged 2,8,8,1. The single outer electron is lost, so Q is a metal forming a 1+ ion.

items.stem: Which statement best describes the transition elements when they are compared with the Group 1 metals?

options.text: They react with water and with oxygen far more violently than Group 1 metals
They have properties that are similar to each other but different from Group 1 metals
They form only one fixed ion each, just like the Group 1 metals do
They have the same properties as Group 1 metals but higher atomic numbers

items.why: The specification states that the transition elements are metals with similar properties which are different from those of the elements in Group 1.

items.stem: Which set of properties is typical of many of the transition elements?

options.text: One fixed ion charge, white compounds and use as catalysts
Ions of different charges, coloured compounds, catalysts
Ions of different charges, white compounds and low densities
One fixed ion charge, coloured compounds and low melting points

items.why: The specification states that many transition elements have ions with different charges, form coloured compounds and are useful as catalysts.

items.stem: Sodium melts at 98 degrees C and chromium melts at 1907 degrees C. Which conclusion do these values support?

options.text: The sodium sample was impure, because every metal melts well above 1000 degrees C
Chromium melts higher because it is the more reactive metal of the two
Melting point depends only on mass, so a heavier atom melts higher
Transition elements usually melt at much higher temperatures than Group 1 metals

items.why: This is the melting point difference the specification asks students to describe, and chromium against sodium is a clear example of it.

items.stem: A small piece of sodium floats on water, but a small piece of copper sinks. What does this show?

options.text: Sodium is less dense than water, while copper is far denser than water
Sodium cannot be a true metal, because every metal is denser than water is
Sodium melts at a low temperature, so a metal that melts easily is light
Copper sinks because it is the harder and stronger of these metals

items.why: Sodium is about 0.97 g/cm3 and copper about 8.9 g/cm3, which is the density difference between Group 1 and the transition elements.

items.stem: Potassium and nickel are each added to a separate beaker of cold water. What would you see?

options.text: Both metals fizz gently, but the nickel fizzes much more slowly
Neither metal reacts, because unreactive metals like nickel show no change
Potassium fizzes and melts; the nickel does not change
The nickel fizzes strongly while the potassium slowly darkens

items.why: Potassium reacts vigorously with cold water, releasing hydrogen and melting from the heat given out, while nickel shows no visible reaction.

items.stem: Freshly cut sodium and freshly polished copper are both left out in air. What happens to their shiny surfaces?

options.text: The copper stays shiny for ever, because it never reacts with oxygen
The sodium stays shiny, while the copper dulls in a few seconds
Both dull at the same rate, since both of them react with oxygen
The sodium dulls within seconds; the copper only dulls slowly over months

items.why: A cut surface of sodium is coated with oxide almost at once, whereas copper reacts with oxygen very slowly unless it is heated strongly.

items.stem: Sodium and iron are each heated in chlorine gas. Which statement about these two reactions is correct?

options.text: Sodium reacts violently, while iron reacts less readily to give FeCl3
Iron reacts far more violently, because it is the harder, stronger metal
Only sodium reacts, as transition metals never react with halogens
Both react at the same rate, because chlorine is very reactive

items.why: Group 1 metals react vigorously with halogens; hot iron reacts less readily, forming iron(III) chloride, 2Fe + 3Cl2 gives 2FeCl3.

items.stem: Copper(II) sulfate solution is blue, but sodium sulfate solution is colourless. What is the best explanation?

options.text: Copper is a transition element, and its compounds are usually coloured
The sulfate ion gives the blue colour in any sulfate solution
Both compounds are colourless, so the blue must come from an impurity
The solution is blue because copper metal itself is blue

items.why: Forming coloured compounds is one of the properties the specification gives for transition elements, exemplified here by a compound of copper.

items.stem: Iron forms two chlorides, FeCl2 and FeCl3. What does the (II) in the name iron(II) chloride tell you?

options.text: Two chlorine atoms are joined to each of the iron atoms
The iron atom has lost two protons from the nucleus
It is the second of the chlorides that iron forms
The iron ion in this compound carries a charge of 2+

items.why: The Roman numeral gives the charge on the transition metal ion, which is what lets iron form both iron(II) and iron(III) compounds.

items.stem: Hydrogen peroxide decomposes slowly. When manganese(IV) oxide is added, oxygen is given off quickly. What is the manganese(IV) oxide doing?

options.text: It is used up in the reaction, so more must be added each time
It speeds up the reaction and is not itself used up
It raises the total volume of oxygen that can be given off
It reacts with the peroxide to release the oxygen

items.why: Manganese(IV) oxide is a catalyst, one of the uses of transition metal compounds that the specification names.

items.stem: Sodium can be cut with a knife, but chromium is used for tools and hard-wearing plating. What does this show?

options.text: Chromium is harder, so it is also the more reactive of the two
Transition elements are hard and strong, while Group 1 metals are soft
Sodium is too soft to be counted as a proper metal at all
Hardness, density and melting point are really one single property

items.why: This is the strength and hardness difference the specification asks students to describe, shown here by chromium against sodium.

items.stem: Element X melts at 1495 degrees C, has a density of 8.9 g/cm3 and shows no reaction with cold water. Which element is X most likely to be?

options.text: Sodium, because metals such as sodium melt at above 1000 degrees C
Lithium, because all metals are dense and sink in water
Cobalt, because those values are typical of a transition metal
Calcium, because it reacts only slowly with the cold water in a beaker

items.why: Cobalt melts at 1495 degrees C and has a density of 8.9 g/cm3; a high melting point, high density and no reaction with cold water are the transition metal pattern.
